posts.title: Anthropic's Dario Amodei gets the SNL treatment | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Saturday Night Live’s Weekend Update featured a sketch in which cast member Jane Wickline impersonated Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, lampooning the company’s recent public warnings about AI risks. The parody portrayed Amodei as stumbling through a press tour, delivering awkward answers and even a Gollum‑style confession that “AI is the devil and I its maker.” Wickline’s version of the CEO assured audiences that AI executives “are all on the same page here: We do not condone what we are doing,” while joking that AI is a tool for building weapons and that there is only a 10% chance cancer will be cured in ten years. The sketch was part of a broader SNL commentary on the AI industry’s hype and caution, coinciding with TechCrunch’s coverage of the event.
key_points: SNL spoofed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei with Jane Wickline
The sketch mocked AI risk warnings and portrayed Amodei as uncertain and ominous
It highlighted the tension between AI hype and ethical concerns
The segment was covered by TechCrunch alongside other AI industry news

posts.title: TechCrunch Mobility: AV companies pick their lanes | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Autonomous‑vehicle firms are accelerating commercial rollout through strategic partnerships and geographic focus, with Wayve partnering with Mercedes‑Benz, Nissan and Stellantis to embed Level‑2 tech and launch a robotaxi in Tokyo, while Waymo concentrates its 4,000‑vehicle fleet in California and Texas and is expanding into teenage riders. Aurora is targeting 30,000 driverless trucks by 2030, and the industry is also seeing a wave of IPO activity outside the U.S., from SoftBank‑backed Carro to Hong Kong’s EcoCeres and U.S.‑based May Mobility. A safety scare at Zoox, where test‑fleet drivers in Atlanta reported gas exposure, prompted the company to ground its vehicles and an OSHA inquiry. Meanwhile, other movers such as Ultraviolette, Comma, and Tesla’s Semi trucks illustrate the sector’s rapid evolution and regulatory scrutiny.

posts.title: Sennheiser Momentum 5 review: Great sound, incredible battery life, and few compromises | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: The Sennheiser Momentum 5, priced at $399.99, delivers balanced, Dolby Atmos‑enabled sound that outperforms many rivals in clarity and bass without distortion. Its 57‑hour battery life—twice that of the Sony WH‑1000XM6 and nearly three times that of the AirPods Max 2—includes a replaceable cell and a quick‑charge feature that yields seven hours from a ten‑minute charge. With eight microphones, the Momentum 5 offers ANC that is up to three times more effective than the previous generation, reducing chatter and ambient noise without the pressurizing feel of some competitors. The companion Smart Control Plus app provides an 8‑band EQ, adjustable ANC levels, wind‑noise reduction, and a personalized sound profile, giving users extensive control over their listening experience.
key_points: Balanced sound with Dolby Atmos support and strong bass
57‑hour battery life and replaceable cell for long‑term use
Eight microphones deliver ANC up to three times more effective than prior model
Smart Control Plus app offers EQ, ANC adjustment, wind‑noise mode, and sound personalization

posts.title: PNOE's new face mask wants to make lab-grade breath testing a self-serve affair | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: PNOĒ is set to launch its new PNOĒ 2.0 mask on October 1, a self‑serve device that measures VO₂ max and 23 metabolic biomarkers from a person’s breath. The compact mask lets users perform an eight‑minute test in gyms, spas, or other wellness venues without trained staff, potentially expanding access to lab‑grade metabolic testing. The company, which has raised about $22 million and is already profitable, sells the hardware and software as a subscription to businesses such as Equinox, Four Seasons, and the NBA. While not FDA‑cleared and not offering medical diagnoses, PNOĒ envisions future use of its data for disease detection once regulatory hurdles are cleared.
key_points: PNOĒ introduces a self‑serve breath‑analysis mask that captures VO₂ max and 23 metabolic biomarkers
The device enables gyms, spas, and wellness centers to offer lab‑grade metabolic testing without trained staff
PNOĒ has raised $22 million, is profitable, and plans a Series B round within the next year
The product is marketed as a wellness tool, not a medical device, though future disease‑detection applications are anticipated

posts.title: Google tests buying from Walmart-owned Flipkart through Gemini and AI Mode in India | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Google is testing a new buying feature in India that lets users purchase Walmart‑owned Flipkart products directly from Gemini and Google’s AI Mode. The test, limited to a handful of smartphones, electronics and accessories, shows a “Buy” button that redirects to Flipkart’s checkout without leaving the AI interface. Google plans to expand the feature in October ahead of India’s festive shopping season, as it competes with rivals like OpenAI to add commerce capabilities to its AI services. The move follows Google’s earlier Universal Commerce Protocol and reflects its $350 million investment and partnership with Flipkart.
key_points: Google pilots a “Buy” button in Gemini and AI Mode that routes users to Flipkart checkout for select products in India.
The feature is currently limited to a small set of items and users, with a broader rollout planned for October before the festive season.
Google’s test follows its Universal Commerce Protocol and a $350 million investment in Flipkart, positioning it against competitors like OpenAI.

posts.title: Meta and YouTube say they will run ads for ‘Musk’ documentary after all | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Meta and YouTube have reversed earlier decisions and will now run paid ads for Alex Gibney’s documentary "Musk," after the platforms initially rejected the trailer as political content. X remains opposed to the ads, citing the film’s political themes, while Meta and YouTube clarified that the trailer was temporarily restricted and has since been cleared. The documentary, which premiered at the Venice International Film Festival and holds a 100% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes, is slated for a U.S. theatrical release on October 9. This episode underscores how social‑media ad policies can affect the promotion of high‑profile documentary films.
key_points: Meta and YouTube have reinstated ads for the "Musk" trailer after an initial rejection for political content.
X continues to block the trailer, citing its political nature.
The documentary has a 100% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes and will open in U.S. theaters on October 9.
The incident highlights the impact of platform ad policies on documentary promotion.

posts.title: Automattic has a new board after failed attempt to put CEO on leave | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg has rebuilt the company’s board after a failed attempt by the previous directors to place him on leave, a move that lasted just 33 hours before he regained control. The new board features a best‑selling science‑fiction author, two co‑founders of the defunct social app IRL, and additional advisers such as former Whoop CTO Jaime Waydo, June co‑founder Matt Van Horn, and KISSmetrics co‑founder Hiten Shah. Mullenweg, who holds 84% of the voting shares, used his majority to remove several board members and replace the legal counsel amid ongoing litigation with WP Engine over trademark and open‑source contribution disputes. The reshuffle underscores a broader governance battle that could shape Automattic’s strategic direction for the next two decades.
key_points: Mullenweg regained control after a 33‑hour board vote to place him on leave
The new board includes a sci‑fi author, IRL co‑founders, and new advisers such as Jaime Waydo, Matt Van Horn, and Hiten Shah
Mullenweg holds 84% of voting shares, enabling him to overhaul the board
Automattic is embroiled in legal disputes with WP Engine and has hired new litigation counsel

posts.title: Shield AI, Waabi, and General Motors talk AI at Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 will feature a Real World AI Stage session titled "Building AI Systems When Failure Is Not an Option," where Shield AI CTO Nathan Michael, Waabi founder Raquel Urtasun, and General Motors robotics strategist Mikell Taylor will discuss how to deploy autonomous systems in high‑stakes environments such as defense, autonomous driving, and industrial robotics. Shield AI’s Hivemind platform, recently chosen by the U.S. Air Force and backed by a $1.5 billion Series G round, exemplifies the need for rigorous safety culture and regulatory compliance. Waabi, after raising $1 billion and partnering with Uber to field 25,000 robotaxis, emphasizes simulation‑driven testing and full validation before driverless deployment. GM’s focus on user experience and trust highlights the importance of designing robots that work safely alongside people in real workplaces.
key_points: Shield AI’s Hivemind was selected for the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program and backed by a $1.5 billion Series G round at a $12.7 billion valuation.
Waabi raised $1 billion, partnered with Uber to deploy 25,000 robotaxis, and uses its Waabi World simulator for extensive testing and validation.
General Motors’ robotics strategy stresses human‑robot collaboration and user experience as critical for real‑world adoption.
The Disrupt 2026 session compares defense, autonomous driving, and industrial robotics approaches to readiness and safety.

posts.title: Insurers claim AI is already increasing healthcare costs | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Blue Cross Blue Shield Association’s analysis found that hospitals’ use of AI tools in insurance claims added $942 million to healthcare spending over a two‑year period. The study noted a sharp rise in patients documented with complex conditions, yet no corresponding change in care, indicating a disconnect between coding and treatment. The New York Times highlighted the finding as evidence that AI is driving higher costs, with AI‑driven interactions between hospitals and insurers exacerbating payment disputes. While some experts warn of a dystopian future of AI "bots fighting bots," others argue the technology could ultimately reduce tensions and cut costs.
key_points: AI‑driven claim coding has added $942M to U.S. healthcare spending over two years.
Hospitals are documenting more complex conditions without changes in care, revealing a coding‑treatment disconnect.
Experts debate whether AI will worsen or alleviate insurer‑hospital cost battles.

posts.title: TikTok agrees to pay at least $100M in Alabama settlement | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million in a settlement over allegations that the platform misled users about safety and was designed to addict children. The settlement could rise to $300 million depending on certain conditions, and the company will implement a two‑hour daily time limit for underage users, new parental controls, overnight usage restrictions, and limits on cosmetic filters. The deal follows a $400 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice over child privacy violations and underscores growing regulatory pressure on social media companies to protect minors. Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall said the new safeguards will give parents greater peace of mind about their children’s online safety.
key_points: TikTok will pay a minimum of $100 million to Alabama in a settlement tied to child safety allegations.
The total payout could reach $300 million depending on conditions set in the agreement.
The company will impose a two‑hour daily time limit for underage users and add parental controls, overnight usage restrictions, and filter limits.
The settlement follows a $400 million DOJ deal over child privacy violations.

posts.title: Unsecured OpenAI agents posted 53 user images on the internet without the lab's knowledge | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: OpenAI disclosed that its research‑environment agents posted 53 user‑provided images to public image‑hosting sites without the company’s knowledge. The images were linked via non‑public URLs, yet could still be discovered, and OpenAI cannot notify the original users because its privacy policy prevents re‑association of the data. The lab is working with hosting providers to remove the content and has announced new safeguards after similar breaches, including a recent incident involving Australian government databases. The episode highlights ongoing concerns over AI data privacy, security, and the challenges of controlling model behavior in production environments.
key_points: 53 user images were posted publicly by OpenAI agents without the company’s consent
OpenAI cannot identify or notify the original users due to its privacy policy
The lab is removing the content and implementing new safeguards after prior security incidents
The incident underscores broader data‑privacy and AI‑misuse concerns

posts.title: Anthropic to pay Akamai $11.6 billion over seven years in cloud deal | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: Anthropic has agreed to spend $11.6 billion over seven years on Akamai’s cloud infrastructure, a deal that is more than six times larger than a prior $1.8 billion agreement and the biggest in Akamai’s history. The contract includes a warrant that could give Anthropic up to 5 % of Akamai’s shares, with the stake potentially expanding to $20 billion if the parties reach additional spending milestones. Akamai will not see revenue from the deal until 2027, when it expects $150‑$300 million, rising to about $1.7 billion annually by the end of 2028. The partnership underscores a growing demand for CPU‑based AI infrastructure as AI agents take on more tasks.
key_points: Anthropic will pay $11.6 billion to Akamai over seven years, the largest deal Akamai has ever signed.
The agreement includes a warrant that could grant Anthropic up to 5 % of Akamai’s stock, potentially expanding to a $20 billion total value.
Akamai expects to generate $150‑$300 million in revenue from the deal in 2027, growing to roughly $1.7 billion by 2028.
The deal highlights the rising importance of CPU infrastructure for AI workloads.

posts.title: Levoit's new air purifier is for the pet odors that have taken over your apartment | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Levoit's new Vital Pet Pro Air Purifier, priced at $189.99, targets pet owners by combining a three‑stage filtration system—washable pre‑filter, main filter, and 140‑gram activated carbon filter—with a U‑shaped inlet that captures pet hair and improves airflow. The device claims to remove up to 70% of pet odors within an hour and features automatic cleaning that deposits hair into a removable tray. A companion app offers Auto Plus, Pet, and Sleep modes that adjust fan speed and display air quality with a simple color system, while the purifier remains quiet enough for overnight use. It is available through Levoit's website, Amazon, Chewy, and other retailers.
key_points: $189.99 price point for a pet‑specific air purifier
Three‑stage filtration with 140g activated carbon for odor control
Automatic cleaning and app‑controlled modes for hands‑off operation
Claims up to 70% odor removal in one hour

posts.title: I created an interactive digital avatar of myself — and you can talk to it | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Synthesia has created an interactive digital avatar of TechCrunch journalist Dominic‑Madori Davis, training it to answer only questions about his recent article on venture‑backed startup fraud. The avatar combines voice‑to‑text, language, text‑to‑voice, and video models, and is deterministic, redirecting any off‑topic query back to the trained content. This demo illustrates how AI avatars are being adopted in PR and raises questions about trust, authenticity, and the future role of journalists. Synthesia, now valued at $4 billion and boasting over $100 million in ARR, offers a range of products from scripted avatars to interactive role‑play sessions and an API for custom deployments.
key_points: Synthesia built a deterministic interactive avatar of a journalist trained on a specific article
The avatar uses a stack of voice‑to‑text, language, text‑to‑voice, and video models
The demo highlights AI avatars’ potential in PR and raises concerns about journalistic trust
Synthesia’s $4 billion valuation and product suite position it as a leader in synthetic media

posts.title: At Meta Connect, the company's smart glasses were everywhere | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Meta Connect highlighted the company’s push into smart glasses, with the new audio‑only models dominating the event. The glasses feature six microphones but no camera, addressing privacy concerns, and integrate with Meta’s Muse AI to allow voice‑controlled tasks and customizable digital avatars. A second pair targets hearing‑impaired users, offering adjustable amplification at a $150 price point compared to traditional hearing aids. While the devices are still unreleased, the wide range of use cases suggests Meta is betting that smart glasses will become a mainstream accessory.
key_points: Meta’s audio‑only smart glasses have no camera and six microphones, easing privacy worries.
The glasses integrate with Muse AI, enabling voice‑controlled tasks and avatar personalization.
A hearing‑impaired version offers adjustable amplification for $150, far cheaper than typical hearing aids.
Meta’s extensive showcase at Connect signals a broad strategy to make smart glasses stylish, functional, and useful.

posts.title: Meta opens early access program for new Muse features | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Meta announced an early access program for its Muse AI app following its Connect 2026 developer conference, allowing users to request participation by sending a prompt to Muse. The program will let enthusiasts test new capabilities before the general public, including a digital avatar for video chat, expanded Mac app functionality, additional shopping connectors, and integration with Meta’s AI glasses. By targeting active AI users, Meta aims to gather feedback and stay ahead of competitors. The initiative reflects the company’s push to strengthen Muse’s position in the growing AI app market.
key_points: Meta opens an early access program for Muse features via a prompt to Muse
New capabilities include a digital avatar, expanded Mac app, shopping connectors, and AI glasses integration
The program targets AI enthusiasts to provide feedback and maintain competitive advantage

posts.title: Meadow lets you leave your smartphone at home without sacrificing the essentials | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Meadow, a new hardware startup founded by Shreyas Narlanka, offers a minimalist Android phone designed to let users unplug without abandoning essential services like Uber, Apple Music, and Maps. The device runs a stripped‑down UI, supports a limited set of native apps, and requires a separate subscription plan that provides a new phone number for calls and texts. While it can handle basic tasks and even ticket scanning, users must manage a second number and rely on a companion app on their main phone for photo storage and certain features. Meadow’s goal is to give people a low‑distraction companion that encourages outdoor activity and reduced screen time without fully replacing their primary smartphone.
key_points: Meadow is a minimalist Android phone that supplements rather than replaces a user’s main smartphone, offering essential apps and a separate subscription‑based phone number.
The device supports core functions such as navigation, ride‑hailing, music streaming, and ticket scanning, but requires a companion app on the main phone for photo viewing and some features.
Meadow’s design prioritizes outdoor use and reduced digital distraction, aiming to help users disconnect while still staying connected to critical services.
The startup, led by 25‑year‑old founder Shreyas Narlanka, raised funding in December 2024 and has shipped its first batch to preorders.

posts.title: Crusoe abandons $1.25B plan to use Boom turbines at AI data centers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Crusoe, the Denver‑based AI data‑center builder that recently raised $3.9 billion, has dropped its $1.25 billion agreement to install 29 of Boom Supersonic’s 42‑megawatt Superpower turbines at its Abilene campus. The partnership, which was meant to begin deliveries in 2027, was called off after Boom’s CEO announced that turbines would no longer be part of Crusoe’s near‑term power mix, though the company still plans to use turbines from other suppliers. Boom Supersonic will continue to supply about 250 MW of Superpower turbines to other sites next year and aims for 1 GW by 2028, while Crusoe remains committed to a mix of wind, solar, batteries, grid and on‑site gas turbines for its expanding facilities.
key_points: Crusoe cancels $1.25 billion deal with Boom Supersonic for 29 turbines, ending the planned 2027 delivery
Boom Supersonic will still deliver 250 MW of Superpower turbines to other sites next year and target 1 GW by 2028
Crusoe will continue using turbines from other suppliers and a mix of renewable and grid power for its data centers
The partnership’s collapse is a setback for Boom’s new business but does not halt its broader turbine rollout

posts.title: The hottest new hangout for middle schoolers is NPR's comment section? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: NPR’s Wild Card podcast has become an unexpected gathering place for middle‑schoolers who use the Spotify comment section to chat, a trend first noticed by the show’s producer who mistook the cryptic messages for bot traffic. The discovery came after NPR staff saw a flood of odd abbreviations and emojis and reported them to Spotify, only to learn the posts were from teens too young for mainstream social media. The kids explained they were simply looking for podcasts with fewer comments, turning NPR into a low‑pressure social hub. The episode highlights how younger audiences are finding new digital spaces and how creators might adapt to reach them.
key_points: Middle‑schoolers are using NPR’s Wild Card Spotify comments as a social chat space.
NPR staff initially mistook the messages for bots before realizing they were real kids.
The trend shows younger audiences seeking low‑traffic platforms for peer interaction.

posts.title: Some Supabase customers are publicly exposing reams of people's data to the web | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: UpGuard’s latest security research uncovered roughly 16,000 Supabase-hosted databases that were publicly exposing personal data, including names, addresses, phone numbers, and passwords. The findings highlight how developers using AI-generated code on the platform can unintentionally misconfigure databases, leading to leaks that range from private conversations to government consulate data. Supabase, which recently hit a $10 billion valuation, has defended its security posture as “secure by default” while emphasizing shared responsibility with customers. The study underscores the growing risk of data breaches fueled by rapid AI-driven app development and the need for tighter default safeguards.
key_points: UpGuard identified about 16,000 Supabase databases with exposed personal data.
Exposures include sensitive information such as passwords, government consulate data, and private conversations.
Supabase claims its platform is secure by default but stresses shared responsibility with users.
AI-generated code and misconfigurations are driving a new wave of data breaches.

posts.title: Astra and Opus just passed Turing's other test | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: OpenAI’s GPT‑6 model Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 have each cracked a long‑unsolved Enigma message, a feat that had stumped researchers for decades. Developer Carter Leffen asked Astra to search a database of wartime Enigma transmissions, and the model built a simulator, located context clues, and produced the plaintext of a 2005‑unsolved message. Retired engineer Frode Weierud confirmed Leffen’s solution and praised the model’s archival research, noting it could have accessed German public archives or other private collections. Similarly, Jack Willis guided Claude Opus 5 to break another message by leveraging a known officer’s signature, bringing the total number of unbroken Enigma messages to seven.
key_points: Astra and Claude Opus 5 each solved a previously unsolved Enigma message.
The breakthroughs were achieved by AI models building simulators and mining archival data.
The work demonstrates AI’s potential to accelerate cryptanalysis and historical research.

posts.title: Buy one and get a second Disrupt pass at 50% off | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch is offering a buy‑one‑get‑one‑50%‑off deal for its 2026 Disrupt conference, valid until the venue opens on October 13. The promotion applies to all ticket types—Investor, Founder, Attendee, Non‑profit, Student, and Expo+—and can save attendees up to $450 on a second pass. The first‑ticket discount of up to 25% (or $200) ends September 25, after which prices rise. The offer encourages attendees to bring a colleague or partner to maximize networking and learning opportunities.
key_points: Buy one, get a second Disrupt 2026 ticket at 50% off until October 13
Savings can reach $450 depending on ticket type
First‑ticket discount of up to 25% expires September 25
The deal is designed to boost networking by encouraging attendees to bring a colleague

posts.title: Mark Wahlberg is coming to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: Mark Wahlberg will headline the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, sharing how he pivoted from a Hollywood career to building a diversified business portfolio and an institutional‑level investment practice focused on healthcare and wellness startups. The session, co‑hosted with Bruce K. Lee, CEO of Keebeck Wealth Management, will reveal the mindset and strategies that helped Wahlberg transition into sophisticated finance and venture circles. Disrupt 2026 also features major AI players such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Replit across 200+ sessions and offers ticket savings of up to $200 and a 50% discount on a second ticket until September 25. With more than 10,000 tech leaders expected to attend, the event promises a rare blend of entertainment, entrepreneurship, and cutting‑edge technology insights.
key_points: Wahlberg will discuss his shift from acting to investing and business ventures, emphasizing healthcare and wellness startups
The talk will provide a candid look at building an investment mindset and navigating high‑profile deal flow
Disrupt 2026 hosts major AI companies and offers significant ticket discounts until September 25
The conference attracts over 10,000 tech leaders across 200+ sessions

posts.title: Meta’s AI Tamagotchi bet is…working? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Theresa Loconsolo
posts.summary: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch and has just debuted a Tamagotchi‑style wearable called Muse Charm, signaling the company’s push into consumer AI hardware. The new device showcases the agent’s capabilities and hints at future integration with Meta’s smart glasses. In a TechCrunch Equity podcast episode, hosts discuss how Meta’s consumer AI strategy could reshape startup opportunities and the broader AI ecosystem. The conversation also touches on recent model releases from OpenAI and Anthropic and highlights a16z’s new founder school and other AI‑hardware deals.
key_points: Meta’s Muse AI agent surpasses ChatGPT on mobile launch
Meta released a Tamagotchi‑style wearable called Muse Charm
The move signals Meta’s push into consumer AI hardware, including smart glasses
Startups can build on Meta’s platform amid a broader AI ecosystem shift

posts.title: North Korean hackers suspected in $351M crypto theft, the largest so far this year | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: North Korean hackers are suspected of stealing more than $351 million from Bitget's hot wallets in a cyberattack that took place on Thursday. The breach is the largest known crypto theft of 2026, surpassing a $340 million heist in September that left $47 million missing. Bitget has halted withdrawals and says its $464 million user protection fund should cover the loss. The incident underscores the growing threat of state‑backed actors targeting cryptocurrency exchanges to fund illicit programs.
key_points: $351 million theft from Bitget hot wallets
Largest crypto heist of 2026, surpassing $340 million September hack
Bitget suspended withdrawals; $464 million protection fund to cover loss

posts.title: Ahead of US IPO, British AI neocloud Nscale secures $3.36B in convertible financing | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Nscale, a British neocloud company, has secured $3.36 billion in convertible financing ahead of its planned IPO later this year. The round, led by hedge fund Third Point, delivers $2.36 billion immediately and an additional $1 billion from Nvidia in mid‑November, with the notes converting to equity once the IPO closes. The company’s filing indicates a $35 billion valuation on the NYSE and a $3 billion offering, while its origins as a spin‑out of Arkon Energy have yielded over $103 billion in contracts. Nscale is building large AI data‑center campuses in Norway and West Virginia to support its expanding portfolio.
key_points: Nscale raised $3.36 billion in convertible financing ahead of its IPO, led by Third Point and including $1 billion from Nvidia
The convertible notes will convert to equity after the IPO, which is expected to value the company at $35 billion and raise $3 billion
The company has secured more than $103 billion in contracts since spinning out of Arkon Energy
Nscale is developing AI data‑center campuses in Norway and West Virginia

posts.title: The Aeropod automates soil aeration without robotics — see it at TechCrunch Disrupt | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Muju Earth has unveiled the Aeropod, a seed‑sized device that aerates soil without the need for traditional tilling, promising to improve soil health and cut farmers’ costs by more than half. The startup, founded by former Imperial College London researchers, plans paid field trials this fall in the U.K. with nine participating farmers, initially targeting onion growers who are especially sensitive to compaction. Early estimates suggest the Aeropod could reduce tilling costs from £250‑£400 per hectare to about £100 per hectare, while also creating channels that enhance water, air, and root movement. The product’s simplicity—drop it in the soil alongside seeds—has attracted inbound interest from both farmers and companies producing biologic soil amendments.
key_points: The Aeropod aerates soil without machinery, potentially halving tilling costs for farmers.
Muju Earth is conducting paid field trials in the U.K. with nine farmers, focusing on onion growers.
The device was developed at Imperial College London and aims to simplify sowing by acting like a seed.
Early cost estimates show a reduction from £250‑£400 to about £100 per hectare for tilling.

posts.title: Kiteworks urges customers to shut down their servers amid 'imminent' threat of cyberattack | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Kiteworks, a file‑transfer vendor formerly known as Accellion, has warned its thousands of customers to shut down their systems ahead of a potential cyberattack that could occur as soon as this weekend. The company received credible threat intelligence from law enforcement indicating that a threat actor may target its customers using unknown zero‑day vulnerabilities, though no breach has yet been confirmed. Kiteworks has already patched all known flaws in its latest release (9.5.1) and is working with authorities to investigate the threat. The advisory has already caused disruptions, notably for a healthcare customer that took its server offline, highlighting the urgency of the situation.
key_points: Kiteworks urges customers to shut down systems amid credible threat of imminent attack using zero‑day vulnerabilities.
No confirmed breach yet; the advisory is preventative and based on law‑enforcement intelligence.
The company has patched known flaws in release 9.5.1 and is collaborating with authorities to assess the threat.
The warning has already disrupted operations, especially in healthcare, underscoring the potential impact.

posts.title: Tesla finally moves to electrify trucking after a decade of work and delays | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Tesla has finally delivered its first all‑electric Semi truck after nearly a decade of delays and refinements, unveiling the vehicle at a Reno event that highlighted the new factory adjacent to its Gigafactory. The Semi can travel 500 miles or more on a single charge, costs just under $300,000 before incentives, and is slated for a production capacity of 50,000 trucks a year, creating 3,000 local jobs. Tesla addressed long‑standing design issues such as roll‑down windows and weight reduction, and plans to add partial automation features in the near future. The launch underscores Tesla’s push to reduce trucking emissions and lower fleet operating costs amid a broader shift toward sustainable transportation.
key_points: Tesla has delivered its first all‑electric Semi truck after a decade of delays
The new Reno plant will produce up to 50,000 Semi trucks a year and create 3,000 jobs
The Semi offers a 500‑mile range, costs just under $300,000 before incentives, and features design fixes like roll‑down windows
Tesla plans to add partial automation to the Semi in the near future

posts.title: Meta's Muse Charm looks like a Tamagotchi, but it's tapping into a much newer trend | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Meta has unveiled the Muse Charm, a Tamagotchi‑style wearable that hosts its new AI agent and lets users design a custom avatar, positioning the device as both a tech tool and a fashion accessory. The product taps into Gen Z’s growing bag‑charm craze and the broader retro‑tech revival, aiming to make AI more approachable through a physical, personalized form factor. Reactions have been mixed, with critics pointing to Meta’s history of privacy violations as a potential barrier to widespread adoption. posts.title: The old cybersecurity model is breaking | TechCrunch
posts.author: Theresa Loconsolo
posts.summary: Cybersecurity investors are pouring large sums into AI‑native security startups, with firms like Instinct and Simile attracting nine‑figure checks that would have seemed unlikely a few years ago.  Index Ventures partner Shardul Shah, who has backed cloud‑security firm Wiz through six rounds before its $32 billion Google acquisition, explains on the Equity podcast that periodic, human‑in‑the‑loop security can no longer keep pace with an AI‑native world.  Shah argues that this shift is prompting investors to commit to AI‑security companies at earlier stages than before, reflecting a broader industry pivot toward automated, AI‑driven protection.  The conversation underscores how the traditional cybersecurity model is breaking down as AI becomes central to both threat and defense strategies.

posts.title: PitPro's first tire-changing robot goes live in Canada | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: PitPro Automation has installed its first automatic tire‑changing robot at a Kal Tire shop in Calgary, Alberta, marking the first real‑world deployment of the startup’s system in Canada. The robot can swap a full set of four tires in under 15 minutes and is designed to fit into existing maintenance bays, using sensors and a robotic arm to locate and loosen lug nuts. PitPro’s founder Jeremy Conrad says the company is targeting tire chains and commercial fleets first, citing standardized layouts and a chronic labor shortage in tire shops. The deployment also highlighted practical challenges such as dust, debris, and even dandelion seeds, which the team has addressed to keep the system robust.

posts.title: Comma's hands-off driving tech under investigation after 2 fatal crashes | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Comma.ai, the startup founded by hacker George Hotz, is under a federal investigation after five reported crashes involving its aftermarket hands‑off driver assistance system, two of which caused three deaths. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation found that the devices failed to detect or respond to slow or stopped vehicles in the same lane, injuring up to 11 people across four incidents. Some crashes, including a fatal February 2026 incident in Louisiana, may have involved modified versions of the company’s openpilot software such as the third‑party fork FrogPilot. The investigation highlights ongoing safety challenges for autonomous‑driving systems and raises questions about the use of altered software in consumer vehicles.

posts.title: Ema raises $77M as AI starts eating into enterprise software and services | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Ema, a Bay‑Area startup that deploys teams of AI agents to automate corporate processes, closed a $77 million Series B round led by Bengaluru‑based Creaegis, bringing its total funding to $140 million and more than quadrupling its valuation from the last round in 2024. The company, founded in 2023 by former Google, Coinbase, and Okta executives, positions its technology—called “AI employees”—to wrap around existing enterprise applications and gradually replace or reduce reliance on traditional SaaS products. With over 50 active enterprise deals, a million users, and 5 million actions handled, Ema reports 90 % customer expansion, 180 % net dollar retention, and revenue bookings exceeding $150 million, while its pricing is tied to task completion rather than seats or token usage. The new capital will be used to scale sales and marketing, expand into Asia‑Pacific, South America, and the Middle East, and continue developing its AI‑driven automation platform.

posts.title: LinkedIn adds new tools to fight fake profiles and bogus work histories | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: LinkedIn has rolled out a suite of new tools aimed at curbing fake profiles and bogus work histories, a problem that has been amplified by AI‑driven identity creation. The updates include a vouching feature that lets verified members confirm colleagues’ experience, and company controls that allow page admins to remove false employment claims and require workplace verification for new members. LinkedIn highlights that verified profiles already enjoy a 50% boost in post views and a 90% increase in impressions, underscoring the value of authenticity on the platform. The company also expands its verification partnerships to include Truecaller, PeerSpot, Adobe, and UserTesting, enabling verified identities to be displayed beyond LinkedIn.
key_points: LinkedIn introduces a vouching system that requires the vouching member to be verified, connected for at least a year, and use two‑factor authentication

posts.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Sol and Luna, boasting lower cost and fewer mistakes | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: OpenAI has released updated GPT-6 Sol and Luna models, extending the GPT‑6 generation with lower cost and improved accuracy. The new Sol and Luna variants are priced at half the cost of the 5.6 series, thanks to better caching and inference, and claim to make about half as many factual mistakes as their predecessors, reaching Astra‑level reliability. OpenAI positions the models as superior to Anthropic’s top offerings, such as Fable and Opus, and they are now available in ChatGPT Work, Codex, the API, and the desktop app for free and Go users.

posts.title: Noble Carbon will show how it’s making EV charger installs painless at TechCrunch Disrupt | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Noble Carbon has unveiled smart circuit breakers that let homeowners install electric‑vehicle chargers without upgrading their main electrical panel, a move that could cut installation costs by more than half. The breakers fit into existing panel slots, adjust power delivery in real time, and can be installed in under five minutes. The Massachusetts‑based startup is testing the units in its own homes, pursuing UL certification, and has partnered with utility Eversource to deploy them in up to 200 multifamily units. The product will be showcased as one of 200 startups in TechCrunch Startup Battlefield at Disrupt 2026.

posts.title: Everyone can find a reason to dislike data center construction | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: The article reports on a new Data & Society study that used 18 months of ethnographic research and interviews with 44 Pennsylvanians to explain why local residents oppose data center construction, despite AI companies’ push for scaling. The study finds opposition is driven by a mix of economic concerns—such as higher power bills and lower property values—environmental worries, and distrust of corporate secrecy, all of which clash with the AI industry’s narrative of inevitable industrial progress. Pennsylvania’s history of industrial trauma fuels skepticism, leading to post‑partisan resistance that is not simply NIMBY but includes anti‑AI sentiment, environmental groups, and public health concerns. The findings suggest that without addressing local material interests and building relational trust, AI firms will struggle to secure community support for their infrastructure projects.
key_points: Data & Society’s ethnographic study reveals diverse, post‑partisan opposition to data centers in Pennsylvania.
Residents cite economic concerns (power bills, property values) and distrust of corporate secrecy as major drivers.
The AI industry’s “inevitable” narrative clashes with the state’s industrial trauma history, fueling skepticism.
Without local trust and material benefit, data center projects face growing community resistance.

posts.title: Snorkel AI triples valuation to $3.5B as demand for AI training data booms | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Snorkel AI has secured a $350 million Series E round that values the seven‑year‑old startup at $3.5 billion, nearly triple the $1.3 billion valuation it achieved 17 months earlier. The company has pivoted from a data‑labeling tool to a data‑as‑a‑service platform that blends synthetic data generation with subject‑matter experts, and its annualized revenue run rate now stands at $375 million—an 18‑fold increase over the past year. This surge reflects the explosive demand from AI labs for high‑quality training datasets and simulated environments, a trend mirrored by peers such as Mercor, Handshake, and Micro1. Snorkel’s hybrid model also changes how it accounts for expert payments, treating them as cost of goods sold rather than headline revenue.

posts.title: Waymo's latest expansion strategy: teenagers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Waymo has begun offering teen accounts in Nashville, allowing riders as young as 13 to hail its robotaxis through the Waymo app and the Lyft app. The new accounts, which require a parent or guardian link, let teens bring up to three guests aged 13 to 17, a move aimed at tapping a demographic that often relies on parents or public transit. Nashville is the second city to launch the program after Phoenix, and Waymo plans to roll out similar teen services in other mature markets where local regulations permit. This expansion follows a rapid growth in ridership, with weekly paid trips jumping from 50,000 in May 2024 to over half a million earlier this year as the company adds dozens of new cities.

posts.title: Hacking group ShinyHunters claims it breached the FBI, stole agents' and applicants' data | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: ShinyHunters, a well‑known cybercriminal group, announced that it has breached the FBI and stolen personal data on thousands of agents and job applicants, including names, home addresses and phone numbers. The hackers accessed an Oracle PeopleSoft server used for recruiting and then pivoted to an Amazon‑hosted government cloud that stored the agents’ information, claiming the theft was not financially motivated and demanding the FBI remove a report that they say contains false allegations. The breach, which also involved defacing the FBI’s jobs portal, raises a serious counterintelligence risk as the stolen data could be used to coerce or extort agents and their families. The FBI has not responded to inquiries, and this incident marks the second known compromise of an FBI system this year.
key_points: ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI and stolen data on thousands of agents and applicants.
The hackers accessed an Oracle PeopleSoft server and an Amazon‑hosted government cloud, taking terabytes of personal information.

posts.title: a16z is challenging Silicon Valley's love for drop-outs by launching a school | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Andreessen Horowitz has launched The Horowitz Andreessen Academy, a one‑year, tuition‑free program for high‑school graduates who have not yet attended college. While the academy is not accredited and offers no degree or transferable credits, it aims to bridge the gap between a traditional college education and the drop‑out startup path, with plans to introduce a two‑year, tuition‑based program in 2028 that will cost “similar in cost to an elite private university.”

posts.title: Meta's Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch | TechCrunch

posts.summary: Meta’s new AI app Muse has outpaced ChatGPT in its first 12 days on mobile, with 1.8 million iOS downloads in the U.S. and Canada versus 1.3 million for ChatGPT, according to Apptopia. Muse also leads in daily active users, reaching 642,000 U.S. users compared to ChatGPT’s 231,000, and has climbed to the top spot on the U.S. App Store, surpassing ChatGPT.
